Hello,

I want to be very clear upfront. All the lean code I'm about to discuss is AI-authored. While I'm working to learn lean, my role has been more mechanical, and my understanding of the underlying theorems is still weaker than I want it to be.

However. I think I have something of value here.

Starting early in 2026, I've been working on formalizing papers related to a project I'm working on. Specifically a theory called: DKPS (Data Kernel Perspective Space). Working with Chat GPT 5.2, Aristotle, GPT 5.5, and Opus 5.8 I was able to prove most theorems in DKPS related papers, with the caveat that these theorems had heavy assumptions that effectively supplied well known mathematical results as hypotheses. These are well known results that are not present in mathlib. My attempts to get these models to break these problems down and attack them were unsuccessful...

...Until the Fable-5 model was released. It was able to chew through these formalization resistant theorems and arrive at proofs which I'm able to verify as correct to the extent that they are used in the downstream DKPS results I'm more familiar with and that they remove assumptions. Almost all these theorems are now in a state where they only rely on assumptions explicitly stated in their paper, and all other reasoning has a trace to the lean foundations via mathlib or the new ForMathlib library in the project.

I understand that this doesn't mean that the theorems are in the right form for mathlib, or that they are proven in the most concise way, and I'm willing to put in effort to learn what I can.

The repo where I'm working on this is here: https://github.com/AIQ-Kitware/aiq-dkps-formalization the README should provide decent navigability.

I currently have ~11 high level items that are likely upstreamable after review and polishing, but there are 3 that seem to stand out:

  1. Davis-Kahan / Weyl / Courant-Fischer spectral perturbation stack.

  2. Gram-matrix rigidity.

  3. Rank-controlled PSD Gram realization.

I've reached out and am working with subject matter experts to attempt to help me with this. But I also need to be clear: I'm a computer vision researcher and software engineer with a PhD in computer science. My formal mathematics abilities are limited - albeit growing. I am not seeking to make unnecessary work for maintainers, but I will likely require assistance to land these and calibrate myself on the actual value that they have.

I'm looking for:

  1. Calibration on the significance of this formalization.
  2. Advice on what the first piece to break out for upstreaming should be
  3. Potentially a co-author with more Lean experience to help move things forward.

What the community needs in order to judge work such as this is a Challenge.lean and Solution.lean file with the challenge file just importing mathlib and the solution file importing your code (so that we can (a) immediately see what your claims are in a formal language and (b) use #comparator to check that your claims are valid) and a description of how you used AI in a formalization.yaml file as described in #formalization.yaml .

Note that you are just one of many people coming here, every day, saying "I have got AI to do some Lean thing, and now I need help because I don't know much about Lean but I'm not paying for it", and things like the above suggestions are what might separate your project from the many other projects accumulating in this channel.

See https://github.com/rkirov/jacobian-claude for an example of a recent AI-authored project with a file ChallengeConformance.lean importing only mathlib and sorrying all main definitions and theorems, and solution file ChallengeLeaderboard.lean with all the sorries filled in but now with the project imported. Note that in this case the theorems are enough to prove that the definitions are correct.

Kevin Buzzard said:

What the community needs in order to judge work such as this is (...)

Is there any way to make this quote a required reading for newcomers in this channel? Does Zulip have such a function?

Such information would have been good to see in https://leanprover-community.github.io/contribute/index.html That is what I reviewed before writing anything here.

It would have been valuable to have information about comparator there. That would have given me the info I needed to prepare those challenges before posting. (A basic set of challenges has been added to the repo as well as a formalization.yaml).

In order to focus discussion, I think the first standout result worth reviewing is Gram/Procrustes rigidity. I'm currently working on another polishing pass over the proof itself there, but please propose any challenges that should be added to the existing initial set. The initial set of challenges are:

EDITED (pointing only at leaf challenges):

  • Gram rigidity
  • Weyl eigenvalue perturbation
  • Rank-controlled PSD Gram realization

For a quick sense of the shape of what is in the challenges, I have a "headline" theorem statement-shape from each of the thrusts:

-- 1. Gram  rigidity
-- 𝕜 = ℝ or ℂ, E a finite-dimensional inner product space, φ ψ : ι → E.
theorem ForMathlib.Matrix.gram_eq_gram_iff_exists_linearIsometryEquiv_map_eq
    {φ ψ : ι → E} :
    gram 𝕜 φ = gram 𝕜 ψ ↔ ∃ W : E ≃ₗᵢ[𝕜] E, ∀ i, W (φ i) = ψ i

-- 2. Weyl eigenvalue perturbation
-- 𝕜 = ℝ or ℂ, T S : E →ₗ[𝕜] E symmetric operators on a finite-dimensional inner
-- product space (dim n). The right-hand side is the operator norm of T − S.
theorem ForMathlib.abs_eigenvalues_sub_le_opNorm
    (hT : T.IsSymmetric) (hS : S.IsSymmetric) (hn : finrank 𝕜 E = n) (k : Fin n) :
    |hT.eigenvalues hn k - hS.eigenvalues hn k|
      ≤ ‖LinearMap.toContinuousLinearMap (T - S)‖

-- 3. Rank-controlled PSD Gram realization
-- 𝕜 = ℝ or ℂ, B : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) 𝕜.
-- A PSD matrix has a d-dimensional Gram factor iff its rank is ≤ d.
theorem ForMathlib.Matrix.posSemidef_and_rank_le_iff_exists_conjTranspose_mul_self
    {d : ℕ} (B : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) 𝕜) :
    (B.PosSemidef ∧ B.rank ≤ d) ↔ ∃ A : Matrix (Fin d) (Fin n) 𝕜, B = Aᴴ * A
I have posted the first PR in this chain to get a feel for this process. https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/40567

Jonathan Crall said:

I have posted the first PR in this chain to get a feel for this process. https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/40567

I am not sure I follow how adding this PR relates to the conversation asking you to do a comparator run/ adding formalisation file . And this code is pretty far from Mathlib quality in my view.

It’s a completely different matter really to try get stuff into Mathlib , versus knowing it’s legit or not . The latter is checking if it is merely true , the former is trying to think of the best ways to holistically formalise math.

I did add comparator run and added a formalization file. I understand how a successful comparator does not imply Mathlib readiness.

I took the initiative to create a small PR with just one piece of what I have in order to better learn the standards. It has already been valuable for me because I've learned more about how to better format references and think about theorem placement in Mathlib.

I'm happy to move slower and reduce scope if I'm going too fast, but I also hope to signal that I'm serious about following through on this contribution.

If i may, i think you are exposing too much theorems in Comparator.
If any of those theorems are used by other ones, don't expose them on Comparator. Just the top Level Ones not used by other ones.
It's like a program "main" entry point.
This will simplify eventual reviewers work to understand what you are trying to achieve.

Alfredo Moreira-Rosa said:

Just the top Level Ones not used by other ones.

I've updated my previous comment point at the new challenge files, with Weyl eigenvalue perturbation being the one I'm told is the most significant because it sits on the Courant–Fischer min–max characterization. (Which I am working through the prereqs to understand).

Yep, I didn’t setup comparator in my repo, because it is a bit heavy - needs sandboxing, and I rely on lean eval for even more robust validation (because the comparator setup there is done by lean eval team not my agent). The check you are looking at something cheap AI set up, that can run per PR, but is not proper competitor. Apologies for the confusion.

Ok, now I got my agent to add proper comparitor setup in the repo, that you can copy. It does add another 20min to CI after build - https://github.com/rkirov/jacobian-claude/actions/runs/27518572411/job/81331853314

https://github.com/kim-em/erdos-unit-distance-comparator is another example of (hopefully) a proper comparator setup. This depends on https://github.com/kim-em/erdos-unit-distance which has the actual proofs.

Its so cool to see the unit distance conjecture has a lean formalization now. Formal math feels like its about to take off. Hopefully we get a model with capabilities similar to Fable that's publicly available again.

In the mean time I've been working on incorporating feedback I've seen here into both my repo with the DKPS formalization and working to carefully scope out a roadmap for contributing the most useful parts of these Fable formalizations into mathlib. I've also been working to build my own understanding, and I'm at least at the point where I think I have a decent grasp on the theorems themselves.

@Weiyi Wang has been gracious enough to review and provide valuable feedback on the the simplest PR for Gram rigidity result here: Based on his feedback, I've golfed other parts of the proofs to reduce their size, and write theorems in a way they work better with simp, and also worked to better intuit where different helper lemmas should be placed.

Once that receives the necessary core maintainer reviews and any other issues are addressed, I've queued up two follow on PRs. Currently they are drafts because each depends on the previous, but they pass CI, but I'm at the point where I can no longer improve them without external feedback. Is the protocol to keep them drafts until all the blockers are merged, or mark them for review even though their diff contains PRs they depend on?

The PR for the Courant-Fischer min-max theorem and Weyl inequality. It's possible that this one could be broken up into two smaller PRs, one for the min-max theorem and one for the Weyl inequality, but they seem closely enough related that it felt ok to put them in the same PR. There are a few design decisions and placements of helper lemmas I'm still not sure about in terms of where they go.

These set the stage for the more exciting result: The PR for the Davis-Kahan bound on eigenspaces: This is the theorem that I think requires mythos-class models - at least if they are being done by someone who has little ability to provide insight on proof strategy. From what I understand this theorem is a blocker for formalization of many results in spectral perturbation theory.

I do have more results in my ForMathlib folder, including Berge's maximum theorem, but I'm still working on putting that one into its most general form. And I'm also trying not to get too ahead of myself. Having the barrier to entry for formalization lowered like this has been so exciting for me, but I also understand how much extra pressure this puts on reviewers and maintainers. So for now I'm just going to wait my turn in the queue and continue working to build my own understanding, but I did want to provide this update.

Hi @Jonathan Crall , I’d be excited to see an implementation of the key results in matrix perturbation theory (e.g. Davis-Kahan). Sorry if I missed this, but is there an easy-to-read statement/citation for the version of DK you have formalised? I ran a reading group on this theorem a few months ago, the statements and proofs differ and are not always great. I’m also a bit surprised that “mythos-level” AI is required, the proof isn’t necessarily very hard (it depends what you’ve proved!). I have no Mathlib authority, but I’d be happy to help if you’re looking for input from potential users.

Hi @Patrick Rubin-Delanchy

I'm no mathlib expert either, and my claim that it required mythos level AI to get is because I spent a good deal of time with GPT 5.4, 5.5 and Opus 4.7, 4.8 (model numbers from memory, not authoritative) working to get the DKPS proof free of non canonical assumptions, and they kept failing to build out the necessary pipeline of results to get there. It's possible that if I were to break down the problem so these models could attempt the proof in isolation then they would be able to get it, but I haven't tested that. (Although that might be worthwhile to attempt while its likely the models aren't polluted by having this proof in their training data, that would certainly add weight to the claim - or at least shed light on what's actually happening).

Where Fable really impressed me was when I had this hodgepodge of half complete results, and with one prompt it got the entire thing working end-to-end (using a large chunk of my token budget). It wasn't polished - and there is still a good deal of polish to be had - but it compiled. My sense after working with these models a bit is that Fable 5 is very strong as scoping and building plans, while Opus 4.8 and GPT 5.5 can often execute a well-scoped plan, their ability to see the bigger picture is much more limited, and my guess is that was the real blocker. But honestly, I'm still not calibrated on the difficulty of this; its all still very difficult for me - although I have made good progress on building the higher level map of what's happening.

The version of Davis-Kahan I have is the sin-theta theorem. And I (well, opus under my direction) just improved it from a loose version to the sharp version by dropping a dimension factor. It's likely that the proof itself isn't a "Book" proof, but to the degree I understand the theorems, the theorem's signature / API looks decent to me.

If you have any feedback on if there is a more natural way to state any of the theorems (or just any LLM weirdness that stands out to an expert), that would be a big help. Using AI to learn formal mathematics has been such a whirlwind, my understanding is better than it has ever been and growing faster than it ever has, but I lack the experience to recognize when its adding in imaginary details that it got caught up on (e.g. because of a motivating line in a paper the LLMs got caught up with pairing the idea of Procrustes optimization with Gram Rigidity, and just kept incorrectly slipping in Procrustes as synonym for Gram rigidity, and I didn't catch it until @WanWeiLee made a comment about it)

But on DK forms, I have:

  • the overlap form, which works if you have pairwise inner-products of eigenbasis vectors.
  • the projector form, which works when you have the basis independent projector operators.

Citations:
Davis , *The rotation of eigenvectors by a perturbation. (1963)

Yu, Wang & Samworth, *A useful variant of the Davis–Kahan theorem for statisticians*, Biometrika **102** (2015)

Link to relevant theorem: gh-permalink:ForMathlib/Analysis/InnerProductSpace/DavisKahan.lean#L138

At this point, I'm working to build my understanding of Lean well enough to where I could do the Gram rigidity proof by hand, and get to the point where I understand every line, which I hope will let me become a more effective mathlib contributor.

Ok, thanks I’ll have a look. If I’m not mistaken the two papers you’ve referenced have slightly different statements, and are both about sin theta. There’s no LaTeX/PDF explaining? If not, no worries, it’s just that I don’t read lean as easily as written maths…

Thanks for that. Two thoughts (completely subjective):

  1. I think of DK as a theory, as much as a theorem. Really, I think the magic is in the definition of the sin theta distance itself, and its various equivalent interpretations (eg canonical angles, distance between associated projections, a sort of multidimensional cosine similarity), rather than in the theorem (not denying its usefulness)
  2. As I mentioned earlier, there have been small mistakes in the statements and proofs of the result, and (perhaps just to me) some strange mathematical arguments. So I think there is real opportunity for a formalisation effort to make the whole theory a lot tidier.

D’you think your work could be a good base around which to get some experts together to discuss what the structure of the theory should be?

D’you think your work could be a good base around which to get some experts together to discuss what the structure of the theory should be?

Yes, that would be very helpful. In the meantime I'm working on expanding the Davis-Kahan proofs to close the gaps between the formalization and the classical literature. I am sticking only to the finite dimensional cases, but the repo has taken some big steps towards all of the classical DK theorems. I've been able to find other LLM proofs online to help with some of the prereqs, but there still seem to of prior work that is not built yet. It seems to be getting close to the projective form though. From there I might try an infinite Hilbert space result, but we have to see how much longer it takes to finalize the finite cases.

@Patrick Rubin-Delanchy

I spoke with Carey Priebe with regards to this work, and he mentioned that I should connect with you. Small world. I wanted to provide an update. I looks like we currently have the infinite Hilbert space result for bounded sin theta and the other trigonometric theorems, as well as specializations of those in the finite case that do not depend on the infinite case. We are still working towards the full unbounded cases for these theorems. The goal is a full formalization of the entire 1970 Davis Kahan paper. I'm not sure if we are going to get all of it, but we have a sizable chunk, certainly enough for a large number of downstream uses. But to get this into working shape, having some expert input would be very helpful.
